sections.title: A house for arguing about God
sections.intro_md:
In 1575 the Mughal emperor Akbar built a hall at his new capital, Fatehpur Sikri, and called it the **Ibadat Khana**, the House of Worship. It began as a place for Sunni scholars to debate on Thursday nights. Within a few years Akbar had widened the guest list: Shia scholars, Brahmins, Jain monks, Zoroastrian priests and, from 1580, Jesuit priests from Goa. The debates got loud. Akbar kept listening.

Three centuries later, in a lecture hall in London in 1870, a German scholar of Sanskrit named **Friedrich Max Müller** gave the idea a slogan. Of religion, he said, as of language: **he who knows one, knows none**. You cannot understand your own faith, or anyone's, until you have something to set it beside.

That is today's subject. Not which religion is true, but how to look at many of them side by side without cheating: how scholars define religion, how they compare a rosary with a japa mala or the Hajj with the Kumbh Mela, what they got badly wrong, and what a careful comparer does differently. India runs through all of it, because few places on Earth have argued about religion this long, in this many languages.

spotlights.name: The Ibadat Khana
spotlights.spot_it: In the painting: an emperor on a raised seat, Jesuits in black robes on one side, turbaned scholars on the other, books open between them.
spotlights.story_md: Akbar built the House of Worship in **1575** for Islamic debate and slowly opened it to Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians, Christians and even unbelievers. The Jesuit priests Rodolfo Acquaviva and Francisco Henriques reached the court in 1580. For centuries nobody knew exactly where the hall stood. Only in the early 1980s did archaeologist **K. K. Muhammed** excavate steps, platforms and a wall that matched a Mughal painting of the building. The debates fed Akbar's later experiment, the **Din-i Ilahi** of the late 1580s, which historians say attracted only about **18** known members, among them Birbal.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most famous royal attempt anywhere to hear every faith argue in one room, four centuries before interfaith dialogue had a name.
spotlights.memory_hook: Thursday nights at Fatehpur Sikri: every religion invited, the emperor taking notes.

spotlights.name: Friedrich Max Müller
spotlights.spot_it: A clean-shaven Victorian don with thick swept-back hair; in Vanity Fair's 1875 cartoon he holds a book under the caption about 'the science of language'.
spotlights.story_md: Born in Dessau in **1823**, Müller spent his life in Oxford editing the **Rigveda** (1849 to 1874) and directing the **Sacred Books of the East**, 50 volumes of Asian scriptures in English. His 1870 lectures, printed as *Introduction to the Science of Religion*, gave the field its motto, *he who knows one, knows none*. He lost the 1860 election for Oxford's Sanskrit chair to Monier Monier-Williams, partly because he was German and Lutheran. He never travelled to India, yet Vivekananda lunched with him on 28 May 1896, and the Goethe-Institut's centres in India are still called **Max Mueller Bhavan**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He turned 'comparative religion' from a hobby of missionaries into a university subject with its own texts and methods.
spotlights.memory_hook: Know one, know none: Müller's six-word motto.

sections.title: The world's faiths in eight numbers
sections.intro_md:
Comparative religion, also called the study of religions or religious studies, describes and compares beliefs, practices, texts, places and institutions across traditions. It is different from theology, which works from inside one faith and asks what is true. A religious studies scholar can be devout, sceptical or anything between; the method asks them to set that aside while they describe.

The raw material is enormous. In June 2025 the Pew Research Center published its largest count yet, drawing on more than 2,700 censuses and surveys. In 2020, **Christians** were 2.3 billion people (28.8% of humanity), **Muslims** 25.6%, the **religiously unaffiliated** 24.2%, **Hindus** 14.9% (1.2 billion), **Buddhists** 4.1%, and **Jews** about 14.8 million. Muslims grew fastest between 2010 and 2020, adding 347 million people, more than all other religions combined. Buddhists were the only major group to shrink in number.

Two cautions from the start. First, these boxes are modern: the words *Hinduism* and *Buddhism* only came into use in the early 19th century. Second, the boxes hide overlap. In India, as you will see, 77% of Muslims tell surveyors they believe in karma.

spotlights.name: A name given from outside
spotlights.spot_it: A word test: ask what a tradition called itself before outsiders named it. Sanatana dharma, the Way, the Path, the Law.
spotlights.story_md: *Hindu* began as a geographic word: Persian speakers called the people beyond the Sindhu (Indus) river *Hindu*. The abstract noun **Hinduism** spread in English in the early **19th century**; one of its earliest known users was the Bengali reformer **Ram Mohan Roy**, whose tomb, oddly, stands in a cemetery in Bristol, England. *Buddhism* entered English around the same time. The Canadian scholar **Wilfred Cantwell Smith** argued in 1962 that the very idea of 'a religion' as a closed system of beliefs is a modern European invention. The exception he noted was **Islam**, whose name appears in its own scripture.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Before comparing 'religions', a careful scholar asks who drew the boxes, and when.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hindu was a river before it was a religion.

sections.title: What counts as a religion
sections.intro_md:
Every comparison needs a definition, and religion has resisted every one. Scholars split into two camps. **Substantive** definitions say what religion *is about*: gods, spirits, the supernatural. **Functional** definitions say what religion *does*: binds a group, gives life meaning, handles death. Each camp has a classic weakness. A substantive definition built around God fits Christianity and Islam but struggles with Theravada Buddhism or Jainism, which do not centre on a creator. A functional one can sweep in football fandom or the nation state.

The pioneers chose differently. **E. B. Tylor** (1871) went minimal: belief in spiritual beings. **Émile Durkheim** (1912) went social: beliefs and practices about sacred things that unite people into a moral community. **Clifford Geertz** (1966) went cultural: a system of symbols that makes a picture of the world feel uniquely real. Later scholars such as Wilfred Cantwell Smith and Jonathan Z. Smith asked whether 'religion' is a natural kind at all, or a category scholars made up to sort the world.

The practical answer most researchers use today borrows from the philosopher **Wittgenstein**: religions share a *family resemblance*, overlapping features with no single one present in all.

spotlights.name: E. B. Tylor and animism
spotlights.spot_it: A long white beard in an engraved portrait; the name attached to the word 'animism' in every textbook.
spotlights.story_md: Tylor came from a **Quaker** family that owned a London brass factory, left school at 16, and got into anthropology after travelling in Mexico for his health. His two-volume *Primitive Culture* (**1871**) proposed a 'minimum definition' of religion, belief in spiritual beings, and revived the word **animism** for the belief that souls inhabit people, animals and things. He also coined the idea of **survivals**, customs that outlive their reasons. In 1896 he became Oxford's **first professor of anthropology**. His ladder from 'primitive' animism up to European monotheism is now rejected, but his minimal definition is still the starting point in many textbooks.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He gave the field its first workable definition and its first big theory, both of which later scholars learned from by attacking.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tylor's test: are there spirits? Then it's religion.

spotlights.name: Émile Durkheim and the sacred
spotlights.spot_it: A bearded French professor with a high forehead; the thinker behind 'sacred versus profane'.
spotlights.story_md: Durkheim, the son of a rabbi from Lorraine, never did fieldwork. He built *The Elementary Forms of the Religious Life* (**1912**) on reports about Aboriginal Australian clans and their **totems**. His definition: religion is 'a unified system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things, that is to say, things set apart and forbidden', which unite believers into one moral community. His boldest claim was that when a clan worships its totem, it is really worshipping **itself**, the group. The jolt people feel at a crowded ritual he called **collective effervescence**, a term researchers still use for stadiums, protests and the Kumbh Mela.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He moved the question from 'is it true?' to 'what does it do for the people who share it?'
spotlights.memory_hook: The totem is the tribe in disguise.

spotlights.name: Wilfred Cantwell Smith
spotlights.when: The Meaning and End of Religion, 1962
spotlights.spot_it: No portrait here; listen for his phrase 'cumulative tradition' in any argument that 'religion' is a modern box.
spotlights.story_md: A Canadian Presbyterian minister who taught Islamic and Indian history at **Forman Christian College in Lahore** from 1940 to 1946, Smith later founded McGill's Institute of Islamic Studies (1952) and ran Harvard's Center for the Study of World Religions. In *The Meaning and End of Religion* (**1962**) he argued that the Latin *religio* once meant personal piety, and only in early modern Europe hardened into the idea of rival systems with names. He proposed dropping the noun and speaking instead of **cumulative tradition** (what is handed down) and **faith** (what a person lives).
spotlights.why_it_matters: He taught comparers to doubt the boxes before filling them.
spotlights.memory_hook: Religio was a habit of the heart before it was a club.

sections.title: Comparers before the discipline
sections.intro_md:
People compared religions long before universities did. The Greek historian **Herodotus**, in the 5th century BCE, travelled in Egypt and simply translated its gods into Greek ones: Amun was Zeus, Osiris was Dionysus, Ptah was Hephaestus. It is the oldest and laziest comparative method: assume their god is our god in a different costume.

India produced a better model early. Around **257 BCE** the emperor Ashoka had his twelfth major rock edict carved across the subcontinent, telling subjects to honour every sect and warning that whoever praises his own sect by blaming others 'injures his own sect very severely'. In about **1030 CE** the Persian polymath **al-Biruni**, who had come to India with the armies of Mahmud of Ghazni, learned Sanskrit and wrote the first systematic outsider's study of Indian religion, often comparing Hindu ideas with Greek philosophy rather than with Islam.

Then came the Mughals: Akbar's debates, and his great-grandson **Dara Shikoh**, whose Persian translation of the Upanishads travelled to Paris and into the head of the philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer.

spotlights.name: Herodotus and the god-swap
spotlights.spot_it: A marble bust with curly beard and headband; the 'father of history' who was also the first famous comparer of gods.
spotlights.story_md: In Book 2 of his *Histories*, Herodotus describes Egyptian religion at length and labels the gods with Greek names: **Amun is Zeus**, **Osiris is Dionysus**, **Ptah is Hephaestus**. He was curious and often admiring; he even argued the Greeks had borrowed many gods from Egypt. But the method assumes a one-to-one match, so whatever did not fit the Greek template vanished. Scholars call this habit *interpretatio graeca*. Tacitus later described German gods 'in Roman terms' as Mercury, Castor and Pollux. The same move returns whenever someone says Shiva is 'the Hindu Dionysus'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the default human way of comparing, and the first thing a modern method has to unlearn.
spotlights.memory_hook: Amun in a Greek toga is still Amun.

spotlights.name: Ashoka's Rock Edict XII
spotlights.spot_it: A boulder under a shed, its face packed with lines of tiny Kharoshthi or Brahmi letters.
spotlights.story_md: After the war in Kalinga, Ashoka had a set of 14 major edicts cut into rock at sites from **Kandahar** in Afghanistan to **Girnar** in Gujarat and **Kalsi** in Uttarakhand. Edict XII is about other people's faiths. The king, it says, honours all sects, ascetics and householders alike, and values the growth of their essentials above gifts. Restraint in speech is the root: one should not praise one's own sect and disparage another's without cause. Whoever does so, out of devotion, actually damages his own sect. Concord is best, so that people **hear and respect** each other's teachings. He appointed officers, the *dhamma mahamatras*, to see to it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the oldest state policies on religious pluralism anywhere, written 2,280 years ago.
spotlights.memory_hook: Praise your own sect by insulting others, and you insult your own.

spotlights.name: Al-Biruni's India
spotlights.spot_it: A turbaned scholar with an astrolabe, usually on a Central Asian stamp or statue.
spotlights.story_md: Born in Khwarazm (now Uzbekistan) in **973**, al-Biruni became court scholar to Mahmud of Ghazni, the raider of Somnath, and followed his campaigns into India from 1017. While the armies looted, he learned **Sanskrit**, studied with pandits, translated Patanjali's **Yoga Sutras** into Arabic, and measured the Earth's radius from a hill at Nandana in Punjab. His *Tahqiq ma li-l-Hind* (about **1030**) describes Hindu beliefs, castes, festivals, calendars and science, and calls itself 'nothing but a simple historic record of facts'. He compared Hindu philosophers with Greek ones and admitted where his informants might be wrong.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is often called a father of comparative religion: an outsider who let insiders' texts speak first.
spotlights.memory_hook: The scholar who learned Sanskrit inside an invading army.

spotlights.name: Dara Shikoh, the mingling of two oceans
spotlights.spot_it: A Mughal prince in profile, pearls at his ear, often shown with Sufi or Hindu holy men.
spotlights.story_md: Shah Jahan's eldest son was born in **Ajmer** in 1615 and became a disciple of the Lahore Sufi Mian Mir. In **1654 to 1655** he wrote *Majma-ul-Bahrain*, 'the meeting place of the two oceans', a short Persian book matching Sufi and Vedanta terms one by one. In **1657**, with pandits' help, he had **52 Upanishads** translated into Persian as *Sirr-i-Akbar*, 'the greatest secret'. Two years later he lost the war of succession; a council declared him an apostate and his brother **Aurangzeb** had him executed on 30 August 1659. He lies in an unmarked grave at Humayun's Tomb.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His translation became Europe's first full doorway to the Upanishads, and his life shows how high the stakes of comparison could be.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two seas, one prince, one unmarked grave.

spotlights.name: The Oupnek'hat
spotlights.spot_it: A Latin title page with a strange word on it, 'Oupnek'hat', a French ear's spelling of the Persian for Upanishad.
spotlights.story_md: The French orientalist **Abraham Hyacinthe Anquetil-Duperron**, who had sailed to India in 1755 as a common soldier to hunt manuscripts, translated Dara Shikoh's Persian Upanishads into Latin. The result, *Oupnek'hat*, appeared in two volumes in 1801 and 1802. The young German philosopher **Arthur Schopenhauer** read it and kept it on his desk, later writing that it had been the consolation of his life and would be of his death. A Sanskrit text had reached European philosophy through Persian and Latin, by way of a Mughal prince and a French adventurer.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows comparison as a relay race: texts move between faiths through translators who each change them a little.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sanskrit to Persian to Latin to Schopenhauer.

sections.title: Making a science, 1870 to 1917
sections.intro_md:
The modern discipline was born in a burst of about 50 years, powered by three things: new translations of Asian scriptures, Darwin's theory of evolution, and empire, which put European scholars in contact with every faith on Earth and gave them a strong interest in ranking them.

Müller's **Sacred Books of the East** (1879 to 1910) put the Vedas, the Dhammapada, the Qur'an, the Zend-Avesta and Confucian classics on the same library shelf. **James George Frazer**'s *The Golden Bough* (1890) gathered myths of dying kings and harvest gods from everywhere and argued that humanity moves from magic to religion to science. In **1893** Chicago staged the first **World's Parliament of Religions**, where a 30-year-old monk from Calcutta stole the show. **William James** turned to the inner side in *The Varieties of Religious Experience* (1902), and **Rudolf Otto** in *The Idea of the Holy* (1917) named the awe at the centre of it: the numinous.

Much of this work ranked religions on a ladder with Protestant Christianity at the top. The next century's method was built by correcting that.

spotlights.name: The World's Parliament of Religions
spotlights.spot_it: A packed hall in Chicago, delegates in robes, turbans and clerical collars on one long stage.
spotlights.story_md: Organised alongside the World's Columbian Exposition, the Parliament opened on **11 September 1893** in the building that is now the Art Institute of Chicago. Delegates included **Swami Vivekananda** for Hinduism, **Virchand Gandhi** for Jainism, **Anagarika Dharmapala** for Theravada Buddhism, the Zen abbot **Soyen Shaku**, the Brahmo Samaj leader **Protap Chunder Mozoomdar**, and the American Muslim convert Alexander Russell Webb. It was not neutral: its Protestant organisers largely expected Christianity to emerge as the fulfilment of the rest. Native American religions, Sikhs and the Latter-day Saints were absent. The next Parliament did not meet until **1993**, a century later.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the first time representatives of Asian religions spoke for themselves to a large Western audience.
spotlights.memory_hook: Chicago, 1893: the world's faiths on one stage, for 17 days.

spotlights.name: 'Sisters and brothers of America'
spotlights.spot_it: A young monk in a turban with arms folded across a long robe, in a photo he signed in Chicago that month.
spotlights.story_md: Vivekananda, 30, had no invitation and nearly no money when he reached Chicago. His first speech opened with five words, 'Sisters and brothers of America', and an audience of about **7,000** gave him a standing ovation of some **two minutes** before he could continue. He argued that all religions are paths to one truth, attacked sectarianism, and became a celebrity; the *New York Herald* called him the greatest figure at the Parliament. Almost no one in that hall had heard Vedanta explained by a Hindu before. Note: no sound recording of the speech exists. The 'original audio' clips online are later readings by other voices.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He reversed the direction of comparison: an Indian explaining Hinduism to the West in its own terms.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five words, two minutes of applause.

spotlights.name: The Golden Bough
spotlights.spot_it: A fat green-and-gold set of books on a grand old shelf; or the abridged single volume that sold in every railway bookstall.
spotlights.story_md: Frazer, a Cambridge classicist who almost never left his library, began with one strange Roman custom: the priest of Diana at **Lake Nemi** held office until a runaway slave killed him and took his place. From there he gathered harvest rites, scapegoats and **dying-and-rising gods** from every continent, arguing that humanity passes through stages from magic to religion to science. The first edition (1890) had two volumes; the third (1906 to 1915) had **twelve**. Poets loved it: T. S. Eliot's first note to *The Waste Land* thanks Frazer. Scholars today largely reject its grand theory, and its cut-and-paste method is the classic warning.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most influential and most criticised comparative book ever written.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twelve volumes, built on one murdered priest.

spotlights.name: William James and religious experience
spotlights.spot_it: A bearded American professor with a steady gaze; the brother of the novelist Henry James.
spotlights.story_md: Invited to give the Gifford Lectures at Edinburgh in **1901 and 1902**, the Harvard psychologist ignored churches and doctrines and studied **individual experience**: conversion, saints, mystics, the 'sick soul' and the 'healthy-minded'. His book *The Varieties of Religious Experience* (1902) listed four marks of a mystical state: **ineffability** (it cannot be put in words), **noetic quality** (it feels like knowledge), **transiency** and **passivity**. He judged beliefs partly by their fruits in a person's life. Wittgenstein said the book helped him a great deal.
spotlights.why_it_matters: James made experience, not doctrine, a unit you can compare across Christians, Sufis and Vedantins.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four marks of the mystic: unsayable, knowing, brief, received.

spotlights.name: Rudolf Otto and the numinous
spotlights.spot_it: A plain gravestone in Marburg marks the theologian who gave English the word 'numinous'.
spotlights.story_md: Otto travelled through North Africa, India and Japan in 1911 and 1912. In *Das Heilige* (**1917**) he argued that at the heart of every religion lies an experience reason cannot capture, which he named the **numinous**, from the Latin *numen*, divine power. It is *mysterium tremendum et fascinans*: a mystery that makes you tremble and draws you in at once, the 'wholly other'. He later wrote *Mysticism East and West* (1926), comparing the Hindu philosopher **Shankara** with the German mystic Meister Eckhart, a pairing comparers still argue over.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He gave comparers a vocabulary for awe that does not belong to any one faith.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tremble and be drawn: the numinous in two words.

sections.title: The comparer's toolkit
sections.intro_md:
After the ranking ladders collapsed, scholars of religion built a set of working habits. Four matter most.

**Bracketing**, borrowed from the philosopher Edmund Husserl's *epoché*: describe what believers do and say while suspending your own judgement about whether it is true. The Dutch scholar Gerardus van der Leeuw made it the core of the **phenomenology of religion** in the 1930s. **Methodological agnosticism**, Ninian Smart's phrase: the scholar neither affirms nor denies God while working.

**Insider and outsider views.** In 1954 the linguist Kenneth Pike coined **emic** (how members understand their practice) and **etic** (the observer's comparative frame), from *phonemic* and *phonetic*.

**Dimensions.** Smart's checklist of seven dimensions stops you comparing only beliefs. A tradition is also its rituals, stories, experiences, institutions, ethics and objects.

**Lived religion.** Since the 1990s scholars such as Robert Orsi and Meredith McGuire insist on studying what people actually do in kitchens and on buses, not just what the scriptures say they should do.

spotlights.name: Ninian Smart and the seven dimensions
spotlights.spot_it: Smart is rarely pictured; recognise him by his method: seven headings that turn any tradition into a checklist.
spotlights.story_md: A Scot who learned Chinese in the British Army's Intelligence Corps from 1945 to 1948, and first met Theravada Buddhism in Sri Lanka there, Smart founded the **department of religious studies at Lancaster** in 1967, often called the first in Britain. He insisted the subject be **non-confessional**, open to every faith and to none. His dimensions, set out in the late 1960s and finished with a seventh, the **material**, in *The World's Religions* (1989), are doctrinal, mythic, ethical, ritual, experiential, institutional and material. They let a student compare a Sikh gurdwara with a Shinto shrine without assuming either is 'really' about belief.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The seven dimensions are still the most used comparative checklist in schools and universities.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seven doors into any faith: do, tell, feel, belong, live, teach, touch.

spotlights.name: Emic and etic: inside and outside
spotlights.spot_it: When a pilgrim and a scholar describe the same act in completely different words and both are right.
spotlights.story_md: Kenneth Pike, a linguist and missionary, took the endings of *phonemic* and *phonetic* to name two ways of describing culture. Take the 41-day **vratham** before the Sabarimala pilgrimage in Kerala: black clothes, no meat, no alcohol, celibacy, barefoot walking, everyone addressed as 'Swami'. **Emically**, pilgrims say they become like Ayyappa himself, which is why all are called by his name. **Etically**, a scholar sees a classic pattern: temporary separation from normal life, a shared hardship, and equality on the road. A good study keeps both columns and never lets one replace the other.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Most bad comparisons happen when an outsider's column is presented as what insiders 'really' mean.
spotlights.memory_hook: Emic is the pilgrim's word; etic is the map's.

spotlights.name: Lived religion
spotlights.spot_it: Look at hands, not books: who cooks, who cleans, what people mutter on a bus or tie to a tree.
spotlights.story_md: Scholars of **lived religion**, among them Robert Orsi (*The Madonna of 115th Street*, 1985) and Meredith McGuire (*Lived Religion*, 2008), argue that textbook religion, the creeds and canons, is a small slice of what people do. In practice a Delhi family might visit a gurdwara for langar, a dargah for a wish, and a temple for an exam, without seeing any conflict. Volunteers chopping onions in a gurdwara kitchen are doing theology with their hands. The approach also brings women, children and the poor back into a field once written mostly about male priests and texts.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It corrects the old bias of comparing scriptures while ignoring the people who live by them.
spotlights.memory_hook: Religion is what people do on a Tuesday.

sections.title: How to compare without cheating
sections.intro_md:
Comparison is easy to do badly. You can make any two religions look identical by choosing the right details, or utterly alien by choosing others. The scholars who thought hardest about this left a short list of warnings.

In 1961 the American scholar **Samuel Sandmel** named the first sin **parallelomania**: piling up surface similarities and then claiming one tradition copied the other. The University of Chicago's **Jonathan Z. Smith**, who never used a computer, went further: comparison is not discovery but a choice by the scholar, so state your question and say what the comparison is *for*.

The Swedish bishop **Krister Stendahl** offered three rules in 1985 that fit on a postcard. And the Boston University scholar **Stephen Prothero** warned against the most comfortable mistake of all, that 'all religions are basically the same'. In *God Is Not One* (2010) he argued that religions ask different questions: Christianity is about sin and salvation, Buddhism about suffering and awakening, Islam about pride and submission.

spotlights.name: Krister Stendahl's three rules
spotlights.spot_it: A tall Swedish bishop and Harvard dean, smiling, often quoted on two words: 'holy envy'.
spotlights.story_md: In 1985, as Lutheran Bishop of Stockholm, Stendahl faced loud local opposition to a new temple of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. At a press conference he gave three rules for understanding another religion. **One:** ask its adherents, not its enemies. **Two:** do not compare your best with their worst. **Three:** leave room for **holy envy**, the willingness to see something in another faith you admire and wish your own had. Stendahl, a New Testament scholar who had been dean of Harvard Divinity School, died in 2008. His rules are now quoted in seminaries, mosques and school textbooks.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are the shortest working ethics of comparison ever written.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ask friends not foes, best with best, and envy a little.

spotlights.name: Parallelomania
spotlights.spot_it: The tell: a two-column list of matching details followed by the word 'therefore'.
spotlights.story_md: Samuel Sandmel coined the term in his presidential address to the Society of Biblical Literature in December 1961, published in 1962. Classic case: in the 19th and early 20th centuries some writers lined up the life of the **Buddha** and of **Jesus** (miraculous births, temptations, sermons) and claimed one story must have been copied from the other. Similar lists still circulate about Krishna and Christ, or Horus and Jesus, often with invented details. A parallel by itself proves nothing. A careful comparer asks: is the match real in the sources, how common is it worldwide, and was there any route by which ideas could travel?
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most common error in popular writing about religion.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two columns are not a family tree.

sections.title: One object, many meanings: prayer beads
sections.intro_md:
The best way to learn comparison is to try it on something you can hold. Prayer beads are found in Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, Sikhism, Islam, Christianity and the Baha'i faith. The English word **bead** itself comes from the Old English *bede*, meaning a prayer, because counting prayers is what beads were for.

The counts differ, and each number carries a theology. Hindu and Buddhist malas usually have **108** beads. The Islamic misbaha has **99** for the names of God, or **33** to be gone round three times. A Catholic rosary has **59**, arranged in five decades of ten. Orthodox Christians use a knotted rope of 33, 50 or 100 knots. Baha'is use **95**.

Now apply the rules. **Likeness:** in every case the hand counts while the mouth or mind repeats, which frees attention from keeping count. **Difference:** what is repeated, and why, varies completely: a mantra believed to carry sound-power, the names of a God who has no image, or a sequence of meditations on the life of Christ and Mary.

rows.Misbaha: Olive wood, amber, date stones, glass

rows.Japa mala: A mantra, such as Om Namah Shivaya
Do not cross the guru bead; turn back
rows.Misbaha: Often 33 each of three phrases after prayer

spotlights.name: Japa mala
spotlights.spot_it: Brown wrinkled rudraksha seeds or pale tulsi beads on a string, with one larger bead and a tassel.
spotlights.story_md: A **mala** usually has **108** beads plus a larger **meru** or guru bead. The practitioner moves one bead per repetition of a mantra, and on reaching the guru bead turns the string round rather than crossing it. Why 108? Explanations multiply: 12 zodiac houses times 9 planets, 27 lunar mansions times 4 quarters, the 108 Upanishads of one traditional list. Shaivas favour **rudraksha** seeds, from the fruit of an Elaeocarpus tree; Vaishnavas use **tulsi** wood. Buddhists use 108 too, for the defilements to be overcome, and Sikh malas often have 27 or 108.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the template the other bead traditions are most often compared with.
spotlights.memory_hook: 108 beads, never step over the guru.

spotlights.name: Misbaha or tasbih
spotlights.when: Common by the early Islamic centuries
spotlights.spot_it: A loop of polished beads split by two marker beads into three sets of 33, with a long leading bead and tassel.
spotlights.story_md: Muslims use the **misbaha** (Arabic) or **tasbih** (Persian and Urdu) for *dhikr*, the remembrance of God. A full string has **99** beads for the **99 names** of God; a short one has 33, gone round three times. A common practice after the five daily prayers is 33 times *Subhan Allah* (glory to God), 33 times *Alhamdulillah* (praise to God) and 33 or 34 times *Allahu Akbar* (God is greatest). Some strict scholars have argued counting on the fingers is better, following reports of the Prophet's practice. In Turkey and Iran fine strings in amber and coral are collectors' items.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Same hand movement as a mala, different purpose: remembering names of a God who is never pictured.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ninety-nine names, thirty-three a round.

spotlights.name: The rosary
spotlights.spot_it: Five groups of ten small beads separated by single larger ones, closing in a loop that hangs a crucifix.
spotlights.story_md: The Catholic **rosary** has **59** beads: five 'decades' of ten small beads for the Hail Mary, each led by a large bead for the Lord's Prayer, plus a short pendant. Each decade is spent meditating on one 'mystery' from the lives of Jesus and Mary. The name comes from Latin *rosarium*, a rose garden. Pope Pius V fixed the standard form in 1569, and Pope John Paul II added five new 'luminous mysteries' in 2002. Unlike a mala or misbaha, the beads organise a set of **stories**, not just a count.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how the same tool can serve narrative meditation instead of pure repetition.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fifty-nine beads, five decades, one rose garden.

sections.title: Sacred places that several faiths share
sections.intro_md:
A powerful way to compare is to stand in one spot and ask what it means to each group that comes there. The world is full of such places, and they are rarely tidy.

Some are shared peacefully, each tradition telling its own story about the same rock. **Mount Kailash** in Tibet is holy to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and followers of Bon. **Adam's Peak** in Sri Lanka has a footprint-shaped hollow that four religions claim. In India, Hindus tie threads at Sufi shrines, and pilgrims to the Hindu hill shrine of Sabarimala first pay respects at a mosque.

Others are shared under strain. In Jerusalem's Church of the Holy Sepulchre, six Christian churches divide the building by a rulebook so rigid that a wooden ladder has not officially moved since the 18th century. Comparers have learned to read both kinds: sharing can mean deep mutual respect, quiet rivalry, or both at once. The useful questions are concrete. Who walks which way round? Who holds the keys? Who is allowed to pray where, and when?

spotlights.name: Mount Kailash
spotlights.spot_it: A lone pyramid of black rock streaked with snow, its south face marked by a vertical gash like a staircase.
spotlights.story_md: At **6,638 m**, Kailash is not the highest peak around, but four religions treat it as the centre of the world. For **Hindus** it is the home of **Shiva** and Parvati. **Buddhists** identify it with **Mount Meru**, the axis of the cosmos. **Jains** say their first Tirthankara, **Rishabhadeva**, attained liberation here. Followers of **Bon**, Tibet's pre-Buddhist religion, honour it too. Pilgrims walk the **53 km kora** around its base: Hindus, Buddhists and Jains clockwise, **Bonpos counter-clockwise**, so pilgrims of different faiths meet face to face on the trail. There is no recorded ascent, and China prohibits climbing it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One mountain, four meanings, two directions of walking: a natural experiment in comparison.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four faiths circle Kailash; one of them goes the other way.

spotlights.name: Adam's Peak and the sacred footprint
spotlights.spot_it: A sharp cone above the clouds at dawn, a line of lights zigzagging up its side through the night.
spotlights.story_md: Near the summit of this **2,243 m** peak is a hollow in the rock about **1.8 m** long, shaped roughly like a foot. **Buddhists** call it **Sri Pada** and say the Buddha left it on a visit to the island. Tamil **Hindus** say it is the footprint of **Shiva**. Some **Muslims** say it is where **Adam** first stood after his fall from paradise, which gives the mountain its English name. Some **Christians** credited it to Adam or to the apostle **Thomas**. Ibn Battuta climbed it in **1344** and described the iron chains pilgrims used. Today crowds climb thousands of steps by night to watch sunrise from the top.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A single hollow in a rock carries four complete sacred histories, and pilgrims of all four climb together.
spotlights.memory_hook: One footprint, four feet.

spotlights.name: The Holy Sepulchre and the immovable ladder
spotlights.spot_it: Two grey domes over Jerusalem's Old City; on the church's front, a plain wooden ladder leaning under a window above the main door.
spotlights.story_md: The church built over the traditional site of Jesus's crucifixion and tomb is shared by **six** churches: Catholic, Greek Orthodox, Armenian Apostolic, Syriac Orthodox, Ethiopian Orthodox and Coptic. Who controls which chapel, lamp and hour of worship is fixed by the Ottoman **Status Quo**, set out in a firman of **1757** and confirmed in **1852**. Because no one may change anything without agreement, a small wooden ladder left on a ledge above the entrance has stayed there for centuries; an engraving shows it in **1728**. In 1997 a tourist reportedly hid it, and it was later returned.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that 'sharing' can mean a treaty, a truce and a daily negotiation, all at once.
spotlights.memory_hook: A ladder nobody may move since before the French Revolution.

spotlights.name: Ajmer Sharif Dargah
spotlights.spot_it: A white domed shrine in a crowded marble courtyard, pilgrims carrying flowered chadars on their heads.
spotlights.story_md: The tomb of the Sufi saint **Moinuddin Chishti**, who came from Persia and settled in Ajmer, is one of South Asia's busiest pilgrim sites. Akbar walked from Agra to Ajmer to give thanks for the birth of a son, and Mughal emperors gave the huge cooking cauldrons, the *degs*, still used to cook offerings. Visitors include large numbers of **Hindus, Sikhs and Christians**, who tie threads on the screens and offer a cloth chadar for a wish. During the **Urs**, the anniversary of the saint's death, qawwals sing through the night. Dara Shikoh, remember, was born in Ajmer.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Sufi shrines show lived religion overflowing official boundaries: a Muslim saint venerated by people of every faith.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Muslim saint, a Hindu wish, a thread on a marble screen.

spotlights.name: Vavar's mosque on the road to Sabarimala
spotlights.spot_it: Pilgrims in black dhotis with bundles on their heads, faces smeared with colour, dancing outside a small mosque before the climb.
spotlights.story_md: Before they climb to the hill shrine of **Ayyappa** at Sabarimala, millions of Hindu pilgrims stop at **Erumeli**, where a mosque dedicated to **Vavar** stands opposite an Ayyappa temple. Tradition says Vavar was a Muslim companion, once a rival, of Ayyappa, and at Sabarimala itself a small shrine called **Vavarnada** stands next to the main temple. The mosque welcomes the pilgrims, who circle it before continuing. Historians debate who Vavar was. For the comparer, the custom shows how a single pilgrimage can fold two religious identities into one sacred route.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest Indian example of a ritual that needs two religions to be complete.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ayyappa's path runs through a mosque.

sections.title: Pilgrimage and the power of the crowd
sections.intro_md:
Almost every religion sends people on journeys, and pilgrimage is one of the richest fields for comparison because it has so many dimensions at once: a sacred place, a story about it, a set of rules for the road, a shared hardship, and a crowd.

The anthropologist **Victor Turner** argued in the 1960s and 1970s that pilgrims enter a **liminal** state, outside normal life, where ranks dissolve into what he called **communitas**: a feeling of raw equality and togetherness. Hajj pilgrims all wear the same unstitched white cloth, the ihram; Sabarimala pilgrims all wear black and are all called Swami. Critics such as John Eade and Michael Sallnow replied in 1991 that pilgrimage sites are arenas of competing claims. Both are right. The biggest gatherings on Earth are religious. The Maha Kumbh at Prayagraj in 2025 claimed more than 660 million visits over 45 days. The Hajj, limited by Saudi quotas, drew 1.71 million pilgrims in 2026. Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha is said to have woken up, shows the other side of Turner's coin: a century-long dispute over who should run it.

visual.title: Hajj pilgrims, by year (Saudi official figures)

spotlights.name: Kumbh Mela
spotlights.spot_it: A temporary city of tents on a river sandbank, pontoon bridges, ash-smeared Naga sadhus running into the water at dawn.
spotlights.story_md: The Kumbh Mela rotates between **Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik**, tied to a myth of drops of the nectar of immortality falling at four places. UNESCO listed it as intangible heritage in 2017. The 2025 **Maha Kumbh** at the confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna ran 45 days on a temporary city of about **4,000 hectares**; officials said more than **660 million** people bathed, a figure *The Economist* called implausible. On **29 January 2025** a crowd crush killed at least **30** people by the official count; a report based on hospital and police records put the toll at least 79. Here is Durkheim's collective effervescence at a scale he never imagined.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the largest human gathering ever recorded, and a test of every theory about crowds and the sacred.
spotlights.memory_hook: A city for 45 days, a crowd nearly twice the population of the United States.

spotlights.name: The Hajj
spotlights.spot_it: A sea of white around a black cube draped in cloth with a gold-embroidered band, everyone moving anticlockwise.
spotlights.story_md: Every adult Muslim who is physically and financially able is obliged to make the pilgrimage to **Mecca** once in a lifetime. Men put on **ihram**, two unstitched white sheets, so that rich and poor look alike. Pilgrims circle the **Kaaba** seven times anticlockwise, walk between the hills of Safa and Marwa, stand in prayer at **Arafat**, and throw pebbles at pillars representing the devil. Saudi Arabia limits numbers with country quotas: about **1.85 million** pilgrims came in 2023 and **1.71 million** in 2026. In 2024 extreme heat contributed to **1,301** deaths, many among unregistered pilgrims.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Hajj is the textbook case of communitas: the same clothes, the same acts, the same day.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two white sheets erase a bank balance.

spotlights.name: Bodh Gaya and the Mahabodhi dispute
spotlights.spot_it: A 55 m brick pyramid tower studded with niches, a bodhi tree behind it hung with prayer flags.
spotlights.story_md: The **Mahabodhi Temple** marks where the Buddha is said to have attained awakening; it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2002. In **1891** the Sri Lankan reformer **Anagarika Dharmapala** found it run by a Shaiva mahant, with the Buddha image worshipped as a Hindu deity, and began a campaign to win it back. The **Bodh Gaya Temple Act of 1949** set up a management committee of four Buddhists and four Hindus, with the district magistrate as chair. In early **2025** Buddhist monks staged protests and a hunger strike demanding that Buddhists alone run it. Seen comparatively, it is one site, two ways of claiming the Buddha.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shared sacred places are not always shared happily, and law often decides what sentiment cannot.
spotlights.memory_hook: Buddhism's holiest tree, managed by a committee of eight.

sections.title: Rites of passage and the problem of the dead
sections.intro_md:
In **1909** the folklorist **Arnold van Gennep** noticed that rituals for birth, coming of age, marriage and death around the world share a three-part shape. First **separation** from your old status, then a **liminal** or threshold stage when you are neither one thing nor the other, then **incorporation** into the new status. An upanayana, a bar mitzvah and a baptism look nothing alike, yet each moves a person across a threshold in three steps.

Death is where the differences become most vivid, because every community must solve the same physical problem, a body, under very different beliefs about what happens next. Hindus and Sikhs cremate, so the soul is freed and the body returns to the elements. Muslims and Jews bury quickly, usually within a day. Zoroastrians, who hold earth and fire sacred, traditionally exposed the dead to vultures. In high Tibet, where wood is scarce and the ground hard, bodies are given to the birds as a final act of generosity. Mexicans welcome the dead home once a year.

visual.title: Five ways to treat the dead

data.belief: Fire releases the soul; dying at Kashi is said to grant liberation
Respect for the body, awaiting resurrection
Do not pollute sacred earth and fire
The body is an empty vessel; feed the birds
The dead return for a night; keep their memory fed

spotlights.name: Van Gennep's three steps
spotlights.spot_it: Any ceremony where someone is set apart, waits in an in-between state, and returns with a new name, thread or ring.
spotlights.story_md: Arnold van Gennep, born in Germany in 1873, worked in France as a translator and folklorist and, remarkably, **never held an academic post in France**; his one chair, at Neuchâtel in Switzerland from 1912, ended in 1915 when he was expelled during the First World War. His book *Les rites de passage* (**1909**) proposed the three phases: **preliminal** (separation), **liminal** (transition) and **postliminal** (incorporation). The British anthropologist **Victor Turner** took the middle phase further in *The Ritual Process* (1969), describing liminal people as 'betwixt and between' and bound by **communitas**. A Hindu boy's upanayana fits neatly: he is separated, lives briefly as a student-ascetic, and returns 'twice-born'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a comparative pattern that predicts what you will see in almost any culture's life rituals.
spotlights.memory_hook: Leave, linger, return.

spotlights.name: Towers of Silence
spotlights.spot_it: A low round stone tower, open to the sky, on a hilltop, with no door visible from below.
spotlights.story_md: Zoroastrians hold earth, water and fire sacred and believe a corpse pollutes them. The traditional answer was the **dakhma**, a round platform where bodies are exposed so vultures can strip them; bones are later swept into a central pit. Herodotus mentioned Persian exposure of the dead in the 5th century BCE. In Iran the towers fell out of use in the 20th century. In India the **Parsis** kept them, but India's vultures crashed by **more than 97%** by 2008, poisoned by the cattle painkiller diclofenac. Mumbai's community has tried **solar concentrators** and debated captive breeding, while many families now choose cremation.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a ritual system meeting an ecological collapse, and having to change.
spotlights.memory_hook: A funeral that depended on a bird India nearly lost.

spotlights.name: Sky burial
spotlights.spot_it: Vultures gathering on a bare hillside around a group of men, prayer flags strung between rocks.
spotlights.story_md: Tibetans call it **jhator**, often translated as 'giving alms to the birds'. 'Sky burial' is a Western name. Specialists called **rogyapas**, 'body-breakers', cut the corpse so vultures can consume it quickly. The practice makes practical sense: much of the plateau is rock or frozen ground, and wood for cremation is scarce. It also makes Buddhist sense: once the consciousness has left, the body is an empty vessel, and feeding other beings with it is a final act of generosity. Comparers often pair it with the Parsi dakhma: similar method, very different reasons.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Same act as a Tower of Silence, opposite theology: generosity, not avoiding pollution.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Tibet the last gift goes to the vultures.

spotlights.name: Manikarnika Ghat
spotlights.spot_it: Smoke rising over stacked logs and pyres on stone steps by the Ganga, boats drifting past.
spotlights.story_md: On the busiest of Varanasi's cremation grounds, pyres burn day and night; tradition holds the fire has not gone out for centuries. Many Hindus believe that dying in **Kashi** brings moksha, release from rebirth, and that Shiva whispers the liberating mantra into the ear of the dying. The cremations are run by the **Dom** community, low in the caste order yet indispensable here. Families shave heads, carry the body on bamboo through the lanes chanting 'Ram naam satya hai', and the eldest son lights the pyre. Sacred and profane sit side by side: firewood is weighed on scales next to the pyres.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest case for comparing how a belief about the afterlife shapes a whole city's economy.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Kashi, the fire that never goes out.

spotlights.name: Día de Muertos
spotlights.spot_it: An altar stepped with marigolds, candles, photos of the dead, sugar skulls and a plate of the person's favourite food.
spotlights.story_md: On the nights of **1 and 2 November**, families in Mexico build **ofrendas**, home altars loaded with photographs, food, drink and orange **cempasúchil** marigolds whose scent and colour are said to guide the dead home. Graves are cleaned and lit with candles, and people eat and sing beside them. The festival fuses Indigenous traditions with the Catholic All Saints' and All Souls' days, and UNESCO listed it as intangible heritage in 2008. Comparers set it beside Hindu **Pitru Paksha**, when food is offered to the ancestors, and the Chinese Hungry Ghost Festival.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows death rites as a relationship that continues, not a door that closes.
spotlights.memory_hook: Marigolds light the road home for the dead.

sections.title: Explaining religion: society, mind and evolution
sections.intro_md:
Describing religions is one job. Explaining why humans have them at all is another, and it pulls in sociology, psychology, archaeology and evolutionary biology.

The sociological tradition began with **Durkheim**, for whom religion was society worshipping itself, and **Max Weber**, who asked how religious ideas change economic behaviour. Weber also wrote one of the first big comparative studies of Indian religion, *The Religion of India* (1916).

Since the 1990s the **cognitive science of religion** has asked what features of ordinary human minds make gods easy to think about. Its best-known ideas are that we over-detect agents (better to mistake the wind for a tiger than the reverse) and that 'minimally counterintuitive' beings, like a person who can walk through walls, are especially memorable. Evolutionary researchers ask whether belief in watchful, moralising gods helped strangers cooperate in large societies.

These theories are tested against data, and the data are contested, as two cases below show.

spotlights.name: Max Weber's comparative project
spotlights.spot_it: A heavy-bearded German professor with a stern stare, photographed in 1918.
spotlights.story_md: Weber's *The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism* (1904 to 1905) argued that Calvinist anxiety about salvation encouraged disciplined work and saving, helping modern capitalism take off. He then set out to test the idea comparatively, writing large studies of the religions of **China** (1915) and **India** (1916), and of ancient Judaism. In *The Religion of India* he argued that the ideas of karma and caste made a coherent but conservative system. Historians of India dispute much of his detail, and economists still argue over whether Protestantism caused growth. But his method, comparing whole civilisations to isolate one variable, set the template for comparative sociology.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He showed that comparing religions can explain economies, not just beliefs.
spotlights.memory_hook: Weber asked if theology could build a bank.

spotlights.name: Göbekli Tepe
spotlights.spot_it: Rings of huge T-shaped stone pillars carved with foxes, boars, snakes and vultures, inside a dug-out hilltop.
spotlights.story_md: Built around **9500 BCE**, about 6,000 years before Stonehenge, the site's circular enclosures hold T-shaped pillars, some carved with arms and hands, as if they were stylised people or spirits. Its excavator **Klaus Schmidt** saw it as a ritual centre built by hunter-gatherers, and the popular press called it 'the world's first temple', suggesting religion came before farming. Work published since **2019** found domestic buildings, cereal processing, tools and rainwater cisterns holding at least **150 cubic metres**, so it now looks like a settlement that also had special ritual buildings. UNESCO listed it in **2018**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a live test of whether religion helped cause the first villages, and a warning against headlines.
spotlights.memory_hook: First temple, or first village with a chapel?

spotlights.name: Agents and counterintuitive gods
spotlights.spot_it: No picture here. Spot it in any explanation that begins 'our brains evolved to...'
spotlights.story_md: Cognitive scientists of religion start from ordinary minds. **Justin Barrett**, who coined the field's name in 2000, proposed a **hyperactive agency detection device**: we are primed to see intention in rustling grass because missing a predator costs more than a false alarm. **Pascal Boyer**'s *Religion Explained* (2001) argued that the gods and spirits that spread best are **minimally counterintuitive**: like ordinary people in most ways, but with one or two striking violations, such as being invisible or living forever. Too strange and you forget them; too normal and they are not worth talking about. Critics say this explains why gods are memorable, not why people commit their lives to them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It moves comparison from 'what do religions teach' to 'what do all human minds find easy to believe'.
spotlights.memory_hook: A person who walks through walls is unforgettable.

spotlights.name: The retracted 'moralising gods' paper
spotlights.spot_it: A Nature paper with a red 'Retracted' banner across the top.
spotlights.story_md: The **Seshat** databank, founded in 2011, codes hundreds of past societies on hundreds of variables. In 2019 a team led by **Harvey Whitehouse** used it in *Nature* to argue that belief in moralising high gods appeared only **after** societies became large and complex, not before, contradicting the 'Big Gods' idea that such beliefs helped societies grow. Critics found that in many cases where the data were simply **missing**, the analysis had treated moralising gods as **absent**, which biased the result. *Nature* retracted the paper in **2021**. The debate about whether gods build societies or societies build gods continues.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Comparative data sets are powerful, and a single coding choice can flip a conclusion.
spotlights.memory_hook: Missing is not the same as absent.

sections.title: India, the great laboratory
sections.intro_md:
India is where the world's largest religious majority lives alongside the third-largest Muslim population, and the birthplace of Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism. The 2011 census counted **79.8%** Hindus, **14.2%** Muslims, **2.3%** Christians, **1.7%** Sikhs, **0.7%** Buddhists and **0.4%** Jains. That makes it the best real-world laboratory for comparison anywhere.

In 2019 and 2020 the Pew Research Center interviewed **29,999** Indians face to face, one of the largest surveys of religion ever run in one country. Two findings sit side by side. Indians across faiths say respecting all religions is central to being truly Indian, and **97%** say they believe in God. Yet most people's close friends share their religion, and **70%** say most or all of their close friends share their caste. Pew called it 'tolerance and segregation'.

The beliefs overlap more than the boxes suggest. **77%** of Muslims believe in karma, the same share as Hindus; **54%** of Christians do. **29%** of Christians and **27%** of Muslims believe in reincarnation. **32%** of Christians and **26%** of Muslims believe the Ganga has power to purify.

visual.title: Beliefs that cross religious lines in India (Pew, 2021)

spotlights.name: Tolerance and segregation
spotlights.when: Survey Nov 2019 to Mar 2020; published 29 June 2021
spotlights.spot_it: A big survey report whose headline sounds like a contradiction, illustrated here by a Sufi shrine where every faith sits together.
spotlights.story_md: Pew's survey of **29,999** adults in 17 languages found Indians strongly endorse religious tolerance as a civic value while living largely within their own communities. Hindus, Sikhs and Jains overwhelmingly say most close friends share their religion, and many people of every faith say it is very important to stop people of their community marrying outside it. At the same time, in northern India **37%** of Muslims, **12%** of Hindus and **10%** of Sikhs identify with **Sufism**, and **51%** of both Hindus and Muslims believe in the evil eye. Indian Muslims were far closer to Indian Hindus on many beliefs than to Muslims in Pakistan or Bangladesh.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a model of comparison by survey: same questions, every group, one country.
spotlights.memory_hook: Respect everyone; marry your own.

spotlights.name: Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan
spotlights.spot_it: A tall figure in a white turban and long coat, often with spectacles; the face on Teachers' Day posters.
spotlights.story_md: A philosopher from Tiruttani in Tamil Nadu, Radhakrishnan became the **Spalding Professor of Eastern Religions and Ethics at Oxford** in **1936**, a chair created to bring Asian religions into the university's comparative study, and held it until 1952; he was also a Fellow of All Souls. His *Eastern Religions and Western Thought* (1939) argued that Vedanta could speak to modern Western philosophy. He later served as **President of India** (1962 to 1967), and his birthday, **5 September**, is Teachers' Day. Critics say he presented an idealised, Vedanta-centred Hinduism as if it were the whole.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He was the first Indian to hold a major Western chair in comparative religion and set the tone for how Hinduism was explained abroad.
spotlights.memory_hook: From Tiruttani to All Souls to Rashtrapati Bhavan.

spotlights.name: Ambedkar chooses a religion
spotlights.spot_it: A vast crowd in white before a great white hollow stupa in Nagpur, every October.
spotlights.story_md: In 1935 B. R. Ambedkar announced that although he had been born a Hindu he would **not die one**. He then spent about two decades studying the options, Islam, Christianity, Sikhism and Buddhism, judging each by its teaching on equality, reason and caste. On **14 October 1956** in Nagpur he took the Three Jewels and Five Precepts, then administered **22 vows** to about **400,000** followers, mostly Dalits. Seven weeks later he died. His book *The Buddha and His Dhamma* reinterpreted Buddhism as a social ethic. Conversions continued, reaching an estimated 15 to 20 million by 1959.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most consequential act of personal comparative religion in modern history.

spotlights.spot_it: A large open book under a canopy, a Sikh reader waving a white chaur whisk above its pages.
spotlights.story_md: Compiled by **Guru Arjan** and installed at the Golden Temple on **1 September 1604**, the scripture was declared the eternal Guru by **Guru Gobind Singh** in **1708**. It runs to **1,430** pages in Gurmukhi script, and alongside the Sikh Gurus it includes hymns by **Kabir** the weaver, **Ravidas** the leatherworker, **Namdev** the tailor and the Muslim Sufi **Baba Farid**. It is treated as a living person: it is carried to its bedroom each night in the **sukhasan** ceremony, woken at dawn, and fanned with a chaur. A scripture that includes saints from other communities is a comparative act built into a canon.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that one tradition's holy book can deliberately hold voices from others.

spotlights.story_md: Guru Nanak began the practice of a free community kitchen, and the third Guru, **Amar Das**, made it an institution, requiring visitors of every caste to sit and eat together. Tradition says even **Akbar** sat on the floor and ate langar before meeting the Guru. The **Golden Temple** kitchen is usually said to serve tens of thousands of meals a day, and far more on festival days, all cooked and served by volunteers. Comparers set langar beside the Hindu **prasad**, food offered to a deity and returned as grace, and the Christian **Eucharist**: three religions in which eating together is itself worship, but with very different meanings.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns an abstract doctrine, equality, into a daily physical act that any visitor can join.

sections.title: Myths and misreadings
sections.intro_md:
Comparative religion has its own folklore: confident claims repeated so often they sound like facts. Six worth retiring.

**'All religions say the same thing.'** At the level of ethics many overlap, and the golden rule turns up almost everywhere. But they ask different questions and propose different goals: salvation, nirvana, moksha, a just society under God's law. Treating them as identical is a polite way of not listening.

**'Religion causes most wars.'** The *Encyclopedia of Wars* lists **1,763** conflicts and classes only **121**, under 7%, as primarily religious. Definitions shift the number, but no serious count puts religion behind most wars.

**'Marx called religion a drug and nothing more.'** The famous line is half a paragraph; read it whole below.

**'Hinduism is one religion with one holy book.'** It has no single founder, creed or book; it is a family of traditions given one English name in the 19th century.

**'Buddhism has no gods.'** Most Buddhists live in a world full of gods and spirits; they simply do not make a creator God the point.

**'You can hear Vivekananda's Chicago speech online.'** No recording was ever made.

spotlights.spot_it: A bushy white-bearded man in a frock coat, 1875; the line is quoted far more than read.
spotlights.story_md: The sentence comes from Marx's introduction to *A Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right*, printed in Paris in a small journal with a run of about 1,000 copies. The full passage reads: religion 'is the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world, and the soul of soulless conditions. It is the opium of the people.' In the 1840s opium was the standard painkiller as well as an addictive drug. Marx's target was the suffering that makes the painkiller necessary; he wanted to abolish the conditions, and expected religion to fade with them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A comparer reads the whole paragraph before quoting the slogan, especially when the slogan sounds like a verdict.

spotlights.name: Counting religious wars
spotlights.spot_it: No image fits a statistic. Spot the myth in any sentence that starts 'Religion has caused more wars than...'
spotlights.story_md: Charles Phillips and Alan Axelrod's *Encyclopedia of Wars* lists **1,763** wars across recorded history and labels **121** of them, about **6.9%**, as having religion as the primary cause; a popular version of the claim rounds it to 123, or 7%. Gordon Martel's *Encyclopedia of War* gives about 6%. The political scientist **Kalevi Holsti** found protecting co-religionists was a main cause in 14% of European wars from 1648 to 1714, falling to 0% after 1918. The historian **Andrew Holt** concluded in 2022 that no quantitative study supports the idea that religion often causes war. Religion can still fuel conflicts that start for other reasons.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows why a comparer counts before generalising.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fewer than one war in fourteen is mainly about God.

sections.title: What is happening now, 2025 to 2026
sections.intro_md:
The comparative study of religion is not only about the past. The last two years have produced big new data and big events.

In **February 2025** Pew's US Religious Landscape Study of **36,908** adults found that Christianity's long decline in America had **slowed and may have levelled off**: 62% Christian, against 78% in 2007, with 29% religiously unaffiliated. In **June 2025** Pew's global report showed Muslims and the unaffiliated growing in share, and Africa now home to more Christians than Europe.

The Catholic Church chose its first American pope, **Leo XIV**, on **8 May 2025**, after the death of Pope Francis on 21 April. His first journey, in November 2025, went to Turkey and Lebanon for the 1,700th anniversary of the Council of Nicaea, and included the **Blue Mosque** in Istanbul. In April 2026 he visited the Great Mosque of Algiers.

In India, the **Maha Kumbh** at Prayagraj (January to February 2025) claimed the largest gathering in history, alongside a deadly crowd crush; Buddhist monks protested at **Bodh Gaya** over control of the Mahabodhi Temple; and Nashik began preparing for its **2027** Simhastha Kumbh. The **Hajj** of May 2026 drew 1.71 million pilgrims.

sections.title: How to compare religions yourself
sections.intro_md:
You do not need a degree to compare well. You need a question, a method and some manners. Here is a working checklist distilled from everything above.

**1. Pick a narrow question.** Not 'Hinduism versus Islam' but 'how do Hindus and Muslims in my city mark a death in the first 13 days?' Narrow questions produce real answers.

**2. Compare like with like.** Texts with texts, festivals with festivals, ordinary believers with ordinary believers. Never your saints against their sinners.

**3. Ask insiders first.** Read what practitioners write, visit, and ask. Then read scholars. Then critics. Stendahl's rule one.

**4. Use the seven dimensions.** Check ritual, story, feeling, institution, ethics, doctrine and material things before concluding anything.

**5. Keep two columns.** What it means to them, and what it looks like in your comparative frame. Label which is which.

**6. Weigh differences as hard as likenesses.** And before claiming one borrowed from the other, show the route.

**7. Leave room for holy envy.** Note what you admire. That is where comparison starts to teach you about yourself.

spotlights.name: The golden rule, compared properly
spotlights.spot_it: No image. Spot it in any saying about treating others as you would wish to be treated.
spotlights.story_md: The golden rule is the most cited proof that 'all religions agree'. Compare it carefully and it gets more interesting. Some versions are **negative** (do not do what you would hate, as with Confucius and Hillel), others **positive** (do what you would want, as in Matthew). Some apply to every creature, as in Jainism, where it supports strict non-violence even to insects; some to fellow believers, as the 'brother' of the hadith is often read. And each is embedded in a different goal: liberation, the kingdom of God, a harmonious social order. Hillel added a famous tail: 'that is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Go and learn.'
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the perfect exercise: a real likeness that still rewards attention to difference.
spotlights.memory_hook: Same rule, different circles of who counts as 'others'.

sections.title: Recap: ten things to keep
sections.intro_md:
**1.** Comparative religion describes and compares; theology argues from inside one faith. He who knows one, knows none.

**2.** Christians 28.8%, Muslims 25.6%, unaffiliated 24.2%, Hindus 14.9%, Buddhists 4.1% (Pew, 2025).

**3.** Definitions: Tylor's spirits, Durkheim's sacred community, Otto's numinous. Most scholars now settle for family resemblance.

**4.** Early comparers: Herodotus, Ashoka's Edict XII, al-Biruni, Akbar, Dara Shikoh.

**5.** The founding era, 1870 to 1917, built the field and also its ranking ladders.

**6.** The toolkit: bracketing, emic and etic, seven dimensions, lived religion.

**7.** The ethics: Stendahl's three rules; no parallelomania.

**8.** Patterns that hold: rites of passage in three steps; pilgrimage, communitas and its quarrels.

**9.** Explanations are tested, and sometimes retracted.

**10.** India is the laboratory: karma shared across faiths, Muslim saints in Sikh scripture, a Hindu pilgrimage through a mosque.

side_dish.title: Müller's other science: why comparing languages came first
side_dish.body_md:
Max Müller did not invent comparison for religion. He borrowed it from language, where it had just scored a spectacular success.

In **1786** Sir **William Jones**, a judge in Calcutta, told the Asiatic Society that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin shared roots 'stronger than could possibly have been produced by accident', and must have sprung from 'some common source, which, perhaps, no longer exists'. Comparing words systematically, scholars then rebuilt that lost source, **Proto-Indo-European**, sound by sound. Sanskrit *pitar*, Greek *pater*, Latin *pater* and English *father* all descend from one ancestor; the shift from p to f follows a regular rule, now called **Grimm's law** after the fairy-tale collector Jacob Grimm.

Müller, a Sanskritist, believed religion could be studied the same way: compare the oldest texts, find the family trees, reconstruct the original. He even matched the Vedic sky god **Dyaus Pita** with Greek **Zeus pater** and Latin **Jupiter**, all 'sky father'. That match holds up. But his larger theory, that myths arose from a 'disease of language' in which poetic names for the sun and dawn were mistaken for gods, did not survive.

The lesson for comparers: the language method works best when there is a real family and a real route of descent. Religions borrow, mix and convert across families far more than languages do, which is why the hunt for one original religion failed while the reconstruction of Proto-Indo-European succeeded.

offline_task.title: Compare two places of worship, with the seven dimensions
offline_task.body_md:
This week, visit two places of worship from different traditions near you, say a temple and a gurdwara, or a church and a dargah. Go at an ordinary time, dress modestly, cover your head where others do, take off shoes where asked, and ask before photographing anything.

Take one page of notes per place under Smart's seven headings: **ritual** (what are people doing with their bodies?), **story** (what images or stories are on the walls?), **experience** (what is the mood, the sound, the smell?), **institution** (who is in charge, who volunteers?), **ethics** (what rules are posted?), **doctrine** (what is written or preached?) and **material** (what objects matter most, and how are they treated?).

Then write three lines: one real likeness, one real difference, and one thing you felt **holy envy** for. If you can, ask one regular visitor a single open question, 'What does coming here mean to you?', and write down their words exactly. That is your emic column. Your seven headings are the etic one.
